name: Edinburgh
tagline: A castle on a volcano and closes to explore
summary: The medieval Old Town and Georgian New Town face each other across a valley, so most sights are a walk apart. Climb Arthur's Seat on your clearest day.
seasonNote: August festivals triple prices and crowds; Hogmanay at New Year is another peak.
arrival: Trams and the Airlink 100 bus reach the centre in about 30 minutes.
gettingAround: Walk, but expect hills and stairs; Lothian buses take contactless payment.
cashTip: Contactless cards work everywhere; Scottish banknotes are valid UK pounds.
foodTip: Try haggis with neeps and tatties, Cullen skink, Scottish salmon and a whisky tasting.
buyTip: Tartan and cashmere from mills with Scottish labels, whisky and shortbread.
baseArea: Old Town, New Town or Stockbridge

connections.note: Direct LNER and Lumo trains to King's Cross; book ahead.
Air time only; add airport transfers.

items.name: Edinburgh Castle
items.summary: A fortress on a volcanic crag, holding Scotland's crown jewels and the Stone of Destiny.
items.expect: Timed tickets that sell out in summer; windy and exposed.
items.tip: Book the first slot and be there for the One o'Clock Gun.
items.why: It dominates the city and tells much of Scotland's story.
flow: See the Crown Room and Great Hall.
Walk the batteries for the view.

items.name: Royal Mile and St Giles' Cathedral
items.summary: The spine of the Old Town from castle to palace, with narrow closes branching off.
items.expect: Souvenir shops and street performers on the main stretch.
items.tip: Duck into the closes and courtyards on either side.
items.why: The medieval street plan is intact and full of history.
flow: Walk downhill from the castle.
Stop at St Giles' and explore a few closes.

items.name: Arthur's Seat
items.summary: An extinct volcano in the middle of the city, with a 251-metre summit.
items.expect: A real hill walk of 45 to 60 minutes up; rocky and windy on top.
items.tip: Wear proper shoes and take the gentler path from Dunsapie Loch if unsure.
items.why: The summit view covers the city, the sea and the hills beyond.
flow: Start near Holyrood Palace.
Climb to the summit and come down past the crags.

items.name: National Museum of Scotland
items.summary: A free museum covering Scottish history, science and nature, with a rooftop terrace.
items.expect: Large; easy to spend half a day here.
items.tip: Good for a rainy day; don't miss the roof terrace view.
items.why: It holds the Lewis chessmen and Dolly the sheep.
flow: Start in the Scottish galleries.
End on the roof terrace.

items.name: Calton Hill
items.summary: A low hill of monuments with a classic skyline view of the castle and Old Town.
items.expect: A five-minute climb; busy at sunset.
items.tip: Go at sunset or sunrise.
items.why: It is the best view for the least effort.
flow: Climb the steps from Waterloo Place.
Circle the monuments.

items.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
items.summary: The monarch's official residence in Scotland, with Mary, Queen of Scots' chambers and a ruined abbey.
items.expect: Closed during royal visits.
items.tip: Check opening dates and use the included audio guide.
items.why: It bookends the Royal Mile with royal history.
flow: Tour the state apartments.
See the abbey ruins and garden.

items.name: The Witchery by the Castle
items.summary: A candlelit, oak-panelled dining room at the castle gates.
items.expect: High prices; the set lunch is better value.
items.tip: Book the lunch menu well ahead.
items.why: It is the city's most atmospheric room for Scottish produce.
flow: Reserve in advance.
Order the set menu with Scottish seafood or beef.

items.name: Oink
items.summary: A tiny shop selling hog roast rolls carved from the pig in the window.
items.expect: Sells out by late afternoon.
items.tip: Add haggis and apple sauce.
items.why: It is the best cheap lunch in the Old Town.
flow: Choose a roll size.
Pick a stuffing and sauce.

items.name: The Scran & Scallie
items.summary: A gastropub from chef Tom Kitchin, serving Scottish classics.
items.expect: Popular for Sunday roast; book.
items.tip: Combine with a walk along the Water of Leith.
items.why: It is a relaxed way to try well-cooked Scottish dishes.
flow: Reserve a table.
Try the fish pie or steak pie.

items.name: Grassmarket pubs
items.summary: A historic square below the castle lined with old pubs and terraces.
items.expect: Rowdy on weekend nights.
items.tip: Go in the afternoon for a pub lunch with a castle view.
items.why: A simple place for haggis, a pint and a whisky.
flow: Pick a pub with outdoor tables.
Order haggis, neeps and tatties.

name: Dublin
summary: A small, walkable capital: old libraries and whiskey by day, live music in a pub at night. Add a half-day by train to the coast at Howth.
seasonNote: Rain is possible any day; St Patrick's week in March is a price peak.
arrival: Airport express buses reach the centre in 30 to 40 minutes; there is no rail link.
gettingAround: Walk the centre; the Luas tram and DART coastal train cover the rest.
cashTip: Cards are accepted everywhere; a few old pubs prefer cash.
foodTip: Try Irish stew, seafood chowder with soda bread, a full Irish breakfast and a slow-poured stout.
buyTip: Aran knitwear, Irish whiskey and books by Irish writers.
baseArea: Around St Stephen's Green or Portobello

connections.note: Air time only; add airport transfers.
Air time only; add airport transfers.

items.name: Trinity College and the Book of Kells
items.summary: Ireland's oldest university, home to a 9th-century illuminated gospel and the Long Room library.
items.expect: Timed tickets; the library's books are being removed for conservation, so check what is on show.
items.tip: Book the earliest slot.
items.why: The Book of Kells is Ireland's greatest medieval treasure.
flow: See the exhibition and the manuscript.
Walk the Long Room and the cobbled squares.

items.name: Guinness Storehouse
items.summary: A seven-floor brewery exhibition ending with a pint in a glass-walled rooftop bar.
items.expect: Very busy; the rooftop bar is crowded at peak times.
items.tip: Book an early slot online for a lower price.
items.why: It is Ireland's most visited attraction, with a 360-degree city view.
flow: Follow the floors on brewing and advertising.
Finish with a pint in the Gravity Bar.

items.name: Kilmainham Gaol
items.summary: The former prison where leaders of the 1916 Rising were held and executed.
items.expect: Guided tours only; tickets are released 28 days ahead and sell out.
items.tip: Book the moment tickets are released.
items.why: It is the most powerful place to understand Irish independence.
flow: Join the guided tour.
See the museum afterwards.

items.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
items.summary: Ireland's largest cathedral, where Jonathan Swift was dean.
items.expect: A ticketed, working church.
items.tip: Pair it with Marsh's Library next door.
items.why: It dates from 1220 and is central to Dublin's history.
flow: Walk the nave and Swift's memorials.
Sit in the park outside.

items.name: National Museum of Ireland – Archaeology
items.summary: A free museum of prehistoric gold, Viking finds and preserved bog bodies.
items.expect: Closed on some Mondays.
items.tip: Go straight to the gold and the bog bodies.
items.why: It holds the Tara Brooch and Ardagh Chalice.
flow: See the gold collection.
Then the Kingship and Sacrifice exhibition.

items.name: Howth cliff walk
items.summary: A fishing village on a headland, with a cliff path and seafood on the pier.
items.expect: Muddy and windy after rain.
items.tip: Take the DART train, walk the loop, then eat on the pier.
items.why: It is a wild coastal walk 30 minutes from the centre.
flow: DART to Howth.
Walk the cliff loop and finish on the west pier.

items.name: The Brazen Head
items.summary: Dublin's oldest pub, claiming roots in 1198, with nightly live music.
items.expect: Full of visitors, but friendly.
items.tip: Come for early dinner and stay for the music.
items.why: A reliable place for stew, stout and traditional music.
flow: Find a table in the courtyard or a snug.
Order stew and stay for the session.

items.name: Leo Burdock
items.summary: Dublin's oldest fish-and-chip shop, open since 1913.
items.expect: Takeaway only at the original shop.
items.tip: Eat in the grounds of Christ Church or St Patrick's nearby.
items.why: It is a local institution.
flow: Order at the counter.
Take it to a nearby bench.

items.name: The Woollen Mills
items.summary: A modern Irish eating house beside the Ha'penny Bridge, with its own bakery.
items.expect: Busy at brunch.
items.tip: Ask for a window or rooftop table.
items.why: It serves updated Irish cooking at fair prices in a central spot.
flow: Book or walk in off-peak.
Try the coddle or boxty.

items.name: The Cobblestone
items.summary: A plain pub famous for nightly traditional music sessions.
items.expect: Standing room only later on; drinks, not food.
items.tip: Arrive before 7 pm for a seat near the musicians.
items.why: It is the real thing for Irish traditional music.
flow: Get a drink at the bar.
Listen quietly near the session.

name: Dubrovnik
summary: The walled old town is small, so beat the cruise crowds: walk the walls at opening, swim or take a boat at midday, and come back in the evening.
seasonNote: July and August are hot and crowded with cruise passengers; many places close in winter.
arrival: Airport shuttle buses reach Pile Gate in about 40 minutes.
gettingAround: The old town is car-free with many stairs; local buses link Lapad and Gruž.
cashTip: Croatia uses the euro; cards are common but small boats and stalls want cash.
foodTip: Try black risotto, grilled Adriatic fish, Ston oysters and rožata custard.
buyTip: Local olive oil, lavender, candied orange peel and Pelješac wine.
baseArea: Ploče or Pile for the old town; Lapad for value
via: Often via Zagreb or a European hub outside summer

items.name: Walls of Dubrovnik
items.summary: A two-kilometre circuit on top of the medieval walls, above rooftops and sea.
items.expect: No shade, many steps and a one-way route; expensive.
items.tip: Start at 8 am from Pile Gate and carry water.
items.why: It is the essential Dubrovnik experience, with views at every turn.
flow: Enter at Pile Gate.
Walk the full loop, including Minčeta Tower.
items.best: At opening or the last two hours

items.name: Stradun and the Old Town
items.summary: The polished limestone main street, with fountains, palaces and stairways off each side.
items.expect: Packed when cruise ships are in.
items.tip: Come back after 6 pm, when the stone glows and the groups have left.
items.why: The whole old town is a World Heritage site.
flow: Walk from Pile Gate to the clock tower.
Climb a side stairway and loop back by the harbour.

items.name: Mount Srđ cable car
items.summary: A cable car to a ridge 400 metres above the city.
items.expect: Queues at sunset; closes in strong wind.
items.tip: Ride up before sunset and stay as the lights come on.
items.why: It gives the classic aerial view of the walled town and islands.
flow: Ride up from the station above the walls.
Walk the ridge viewpoints.

items.name: Fort Lovrijenac
items.summary: A fortress on a 37-metre rock outside the western wall.
items.expect: Steep steps; included with the city walls ticket.
items.tip: Visit the same day as the walls to use one ticket.
items.why: It has the best view back to the walls.
flow: Climb from the small cove at Pile.
See the terraces and courtyard.

items.name: Lokrum Island
items.summary: A wooded island reserve 15 minutes by boat, with rocky swimming spots, a saltwater lake and peacocks.
items.expect: No sandy beaches; boats run roughly April to October.
items.tip: Bring swim shoes and a picnic.
items.why: It is the easiest escape from the midday crowds.
flow: Take the boat from the old harbour.
Swim in the 'Dead Sea' lake and walk to the fort.

items.name: Rector's Palace
items.summary: The Gothic-Renaissance seat of the old Republic of Ragusa, now a history museum.
items.expect: A small museum.
items.tip: A good shaded stop at midday.
items.why: It explains how this tiny republic stayed independent for centuries.
flow: See the courtyard and staircase.
Walk the rector's rooms.

items.name: Lokanda Peskarija
items.summary: A simple seafood spot on the old harbour, serving food in black pots.
items.expect: A queue at peak times and a short menu.
items.tip: Go at an off hour and share several pots.
items.why: Fresh, fairly priced seafood with a harbour view.
flow: Wait for an outdoor table.
Order black risotto and mussels.

items.name: Buža Bar
items.summary: A bar on the rocks outside the walls, reached through a hole in the wall.
items.expect: Drinks only, cash preferred, and it closes in bad weather.
items.tip: Follow the 'cold drinks' sign and come for sunset.
items.why: Few places to drink have a better setting.
flow: Find the doorway in the southern wall.
Take a table on the rocks.

items.name: Gundulić Square market
items.summary: A morning market of fruit, dried figs, candied peel and lavender.
items.expect: Mornings only; packs up by early afternoon.
items.tip: Buy picnic fruit before a boat trip.
items.why: A quick taste of local produce in the middle of the old town.
flow: Browse the stalls.
Try candied orange peel and dried figs.

name: Reykjavík
tagline: A small capital at the edge of wild Iceland
summary: Use Reykjavík as a base: a day for the city, then day trips to the Golden Circle, the south coast and a geothermal lagoon. Weather decides everything, so keep plans loose.
seasonNote: Summer has near-endless daylight; September to March is northern lights season, with short days.
arrival: Keflavík airport is 45 minutes away by Flybus or shared shuttle.
gettingAround: The centre is walkable; day trips need a tour or rental car. Check road and weather sites daily.
cashTip: Entirely card-based; you can skip cash.
foodTip: Try lamb soup, fresh cod or Arctic char, skyr and a hot dog with everything.
buyTip: A hand-knitted lopapeysa sweater from the Handknitting Association, sea salt and licorice chocolate.
costNote: Day tours and car hire are the largest cost and are not included.

items.name: Hallgrímskirkja
items.summary: A concrete church shaped like basalt columns, with a tower lift to the top.
items.expect: A short queue for the lift.
items.tip: Go up near sunset for the coloured rooftops.
items.why: It is the city's landmark and its best viewpoint.
flow: See the organ and nave.
Take the lift up the tower.

items.name: Harpa and the Sun Voyager
items.summary: A glass honeycomb concert hall, with a steel ship sculpture a short walk along the shore.
items.expect: Free to enter the foyer.
items.tip: Walk the seafront between the two around sunset.
items.why: It is the best of modern Icelandic design, with a mountain backdrop.
flow: Explore Harpa's foyer.
Follow the shore path to the Sun Voyager.

items.name: Golden Circle
items.summary: A day loop to Þingvellir rift valley, the Geysir hot springs and Gullfoss waterfall.
items.expect: About 250 km of driving, with tour buses at every stop.
items.tip: Drive it yourself, starting early or late.
items.why: Three of Iceland's headline sights fit into one day.
flow: Þingvellir first, then Geysir.
Finish at Gullfoss.

items.name: Blue Lagoon
items.summary: A milky-blue geothermal spa in a lava field near the airport.
items.expect: Expensive, and sometimes closed by volcanic activity nearby.
items.tip: Book for your arrival or departure day, and check its status first.
items.why: It is Iceland's most famous soak.
flow: Shower and enter the lagoon.
Use the silica mask bar.

items.name: South Coast waterfalls and black sand beach
items.summary: A long day to Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss waterfalls and Reynisfjara black sand beach.
items.expect: About 370 km return; dangerous waves at Reynisfjara.
items.tip: Stay far from the water at Reynisfjara and bring waterproofs for the falls.
items.why: It is the most dramatic scenery within a day of the city.
flow: Seljalandsfoss, then Skógafoss.
Reynisfjara and Vík before returning.

items.name: Northern lights
items.summary: On dark, clear nights from September to March the aurora can appear overhead.
items.expect: Never guaranteed; it needs clear skies and solar activity.
items.tip: Check the aurora and cloud forecast; tours usually offer a free retry.
items.why: Seeing the sky move in green is a once-in-a-lifetime sight.
flow: Check the forecast in the afternoon.
Drive or take a tour away from city lights.

items.name: Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur
items.summary: A hot dog stand that has served lamb-based hot dogs since 1937.
items.expect: A short queue at an outdoor stand.
items.tip: Order 'eina með öllu', one with everything.
items.why: It is Iceland's national snack and the cheapest meal in town.
flow: Queue at the stand.
Eat at the standing tables.

items.name: Sægreifinn (The Sea Baron)
items.summary: A harbour shack known for creamy lobster soup and grilled fish skewers.
items.expect: Shared benches and counter ordering.
items.tip: Soup and one skewer is plenty.
items.why: A warming, fairly priced taste of Icelandic seafood.
flow: Order at the counter.
Pick a skewer from the fridge to be grilled.

items.name: Café Loki
items.summary: A family café serving traditional home cooking opposite the church.
items.expect: Simple food; busy at lunch.
items.tip: Try the rye bread ice cream.
items.why: An approachable way to taste old Icelandic dishes.
flow: Take a table upstairs.
Order a tasting plate.

name: Amalfi Coast
tagline: Cliffside villages above a blue sea
summary: Base yourself in one village and move by ferry, not road. Give a day each to Positano, Amalfi with Ravello, and the Path of the Gods or Capri.
seasonNote: July and August are crowded and expensive; ferries and many hotels stop from November to March.
arrival: Fly to Naples, then take a ferry, private transfer or the train to Salerno or Sorrento and a boat or bus.
gettingAround: Ferries are fastest and least stressful; SITA buses are cheap but crowded and winding.
cashTip: Cards are widely accepted; carry cash for buses, beach clubs and small bars.
foodTip: Try lemon everything: delizia al limone, lemon pasta, and scialatielli with seafood.
buyTip: Limoncello, ceramics from Vietri sul Mare and handmade sandals in Positano.
baseArea: Amalfi town for transport; Positano or Ravello for views
via: Fly into Naples, then about 90 minutes by road or ferry

connections.note: Seasonal fast ferries; by road it takes about 90 minutes depending on traffic.
High-speed train from Salerno to Rome in about 2 hours, plus the ferry or bus to Salerno.

items.name: Positano
items.summary: A vertical village of pastel houses tumbling down to a pebble beach.
items.expect: Hundreds of steps, high prices and summer crowds.
items.tip: Arrive by ferry for the best first view.
items.why: It is the most photographed village on the coast.
flow: Arrive at the pier and walk up through the lanes.
Swim or take a drink above the beach.

items.name: Amalfi Cathedral
items.summary: A striped cathedral atop a grand staircase, with the Arab-Norman Cloister of Paradise.
items.expect: The main square is busy all day.
items.tip: Pay the small fee for the cloister and crypt.
items.why: It recalls Amalfi's time as a sea power.
flow: Climb the staircase.
See the cloister, crypt and nave.

items.name: Villa Rufolo and Villa Cimbrone, Ravello
items.summary: Two hilltop gardens in Ravello with terraces high above the sea.
items.expect: A winding bus ride or steep path from Amalfi.
items.tip: Walk to Villa Cimbrone's Terrace of Infinity near sunset.
items.why: They have the finest views on the whole coast.
flow: Bus up from Amalfi and visit Villa Rufolo.
Walk ten minutes to Villa Cimbrone.

items.name: Path of the Gods
items.summary: A cliff-top footpath of about 7 km with constant views of the coast.
items.expect: Uneven and exposed, with around 1,700 steps down to Positano at the end.
items.tip: Start early from Bomerano, walking towards Nocelle.
items.why: It is one of Italy's great day walks.
flow: Bus to Bomerano (Agerola).
Walk to Nocelle, then go down to Positano.

items.name: Capri
items.summary: A day by ferry to a glamorous island with sea stacks, gardens and a chairlift to its summit.
items.expect: Costly ferries and heavy midday crowds; the Blue Grotto often closes.
items.tip: Take the first ferry and go straight up to Anacapri and Monte Solaro.
items.why: The Faraglioni rocks and island views are unforgettable.
flow: Ferry to Marina Grande, then bus to Anacapri.
Ride the chairlift, then see the Gardens of Augustus.

items.name: Fiordo di Furore
items.summary: A tiny beach in a fjord-like gorge beneath an arched road bridge.
items.expect: A long staircase; access is sometimes closed for rockfall.
items.tip: Check that it is open before going.
items.why: A dramatic, quick stop between Positano and Amalfi.
flow: Take the bus to the bridge.
Walk the steps down to the cove.
items.best: Midday, when the sun reaches the beach

items.name: Pasticceria Pansa
items.summary: A pastry shop on Amalfi's main square since 1830, known for lemon sweets.
items.expect: Table service costs more than standing at the bar.
items.tip: Have the delizia al limone and candied lemon peel.
items.why: It is the best place to taste Amalfi lemons.
flow: Order at the bar or take a table.
Try a lemon delight with coffee.

items.name: Da Vincenzo
items.summary: A family trattoria from 1958 serving coastal classics.
items.expect: Dinner bookings fill days ahead.
items.tip: Reserve by phone or online.
items.why: Reliable local cooking in a village of tourist menus.
flow: Book ahead.
Order seafood pasta and the day's fish.

items.name: Lo Scoglio
items.summary: A restaurant on a pier in a quiet bay, famous for spaghetti with zucchini.
items.expect: Expensive; best reached by boat.
items.tip: Book lunch and combine it with a boat day.
items.why: It is the home of spaghetti alla Nerano.
flow: Arrive by boat or taxi.
Order spaghetti with zucchini, then grilled fish.

name: Kraków
tagline: A royal old town with a heavy history
summary: The old town and castle fill one day, Kazimierz and Schindler's Factory another. Auschwitz-Birkenau and the Wieliczka salt mine each need a half or full day.
seasonNote: Winters are cold with poor air quality; December has a large Christmas market.
arrival: Trains run from the airport to the main station in about 20 minutes.
gettingAround: The old town is walkable; trams reach Kazimierz and Podgórze.
cashTip: Cards and phones are accepted nearly everywhere; avoid exchange booths with big spreads.
foodTip: Try pierogi, żurek soup, an obwarzanek bread ring and a zapiekanka in Kazimierz.
buyTip: Amber from certified shops, Bolesławiec pottery and linen.

connections.note: Air time only; buses and trains take 6 to 8 hours.
Air time only; buses take about 7 hours.
Air time only; trains take about 7 hours.

items.name: Main Market Square
items.summary: Europe's largest medieval square, with the Cloth Hall and St. Mary's Basilica.
items.expect: Pricey terraces and horse carriages.
items.tip: Listen for the trumpet call from St. Mary's tower on the hour.
items.why: It has been the heart of the city since 1257.
flow: Walk through the Cloth Hall.
Visit St. Mary's carved altarpiece.

items.name: Wawel Castle and Cathedral
items.summary: The hilltop seat of Polish kings, with a Renaissance courtyard and the coronation cathedral.
items.expect: Separate tickets for each exhibition, with limited numbers per day.
items.tip: Book the state rooms online; the grounds are free.
items.why: It is Poland's most important historic site.
flow: Visit the cathedral and its bell tower.
Tour the state rooms, then leave by the Dragon's Den.

items.name: Kazimierz
items.summary: The historic Jewish quarter: synagogues, courtyards, cafés and nightlife.
items.expect: Quiet by day and lively late.
items.tip: Visit the Old Synagogue and Remuh cemetery, then come back for dinner.
items.why: Centuries of Jewish life are still visible here.
flow: Walk Szeroka Street and its synagogues.
End at Plac Nowy.

items.name: Oskar Schindler's Enamel Factory
items.summary: A museum of Kraków under Nazi occupation, in Schindler's former factory.
items.expect: Timed tickets that sell out; emotionally heavy.
items.tip: Book online several days ahead.
items.why: It is an immersive account of the wartime city.
flow: Follow the timeline rooms.
See Schindler's office.

items.name: Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial
items.summary: The preserved Nazi camp where over a million people were murdered, 70 km west of the city.
items.expect: A long, sobering day; entry needs a booked, named pass.
items.tip: Reserve through the official site months ahead, or join a tour with transport.
items.why: It is one of the most important memorial sites in the world.
flow: Guided visit of Auschwitz I.
Shuttle to Birkenau.

items.name: Wieliczka Salt Mine
items.summary: A medieval mine with chapels, lakes and chandeliers carved from salt, 135 metres down.
items.expect: 800 steps on a guided route of about 3 km; cool underground.
items.tip: Take the train from the main station and bring a layer.
items.why: The underground Chapel of St. Kinga is astonishing.
flow: Go down with the guided tour.
Return to the surface by lift.

items.name: Plac Nowy zapiekanki
items.summary: A round market building whose windows sell toasted half-baguettes with mushrooms and cheese.
items.expect: Queues late at night.
items.tip: The stall with the longest queue is usually worth it.
items.why: It is the city's favourite street snack.
flow: Pick a window.
Choose toppings and eat on the square.

items.name: Pod Aniołami
items.summary: A cellar restaurant on Grodzka Street grilling meats over beech wood.
items.expect: Hearty portions; popular with visitors.
items.tip: Reserve for dinner and ask for the vaulted cellar.
items.why: It serves traditional Polish noble cuisine in a medieval setting.
flow: Start with żurek soup.
Share grilled meats and pierogi.

items.name: Stary Kleparz market
items.summary: A covered farmers' market just north of the old town.
items.expect: Mornings are best; closed on Sunday.
items.tip: Buy oscypek smoked cheese and seasonal fruit.
items.why: A local market five minutes from the tourist centre.
flow: Walk the stalls.
Pick up cheese, bread and fruit.
